table.text: This study was approved by the University of Washington Institutional Review Board (IRB; protocol 00022559).
• Results: 18 participants completed the initial in-person and scheduled at-home sampling, and 16 (89%) completed subsequent remote sampling.
Participants were willing to provide a median of 18 semen samples (range, 2-40) and 18 blood samples (range, 5-40) over a future hypothetical study.

To do this, we enrolled reproductive age men in a dual clinical/remote study in which participants self-collected blood using the homeRNA platform and semen using the Fellow kit, continuously monitored home indoor PM 2.5 mass concentration estimates using PurpleAir monitors, and, in a subset of participants, passively sampled environmental organic chemical exposures continuously over a seven day period using Fresh Air wristbands.

By combining these remote collection protocols, we evaluated the feasibility of a multi-biofluid collection study with multiple timepoints where, during wildfire season, enrolled participants provided one baseline sample in-clinic and up to three samples remotely.

The Fellow Semen Analysis Kit (Fellow) is a semen analysis platform that enables at-home semen collection, stabilization, and shipment for laboratory semen analysis (SI.1)https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?RMhwhy 24,25) The homeRNAmax Blood Collection and Stabilization Kit (homeRNA) combines a commercially available peripheral blood collection device with a custom-engineered stabilization tube (SI.2)https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Hqmpgm Fresh Air wristbands (FAW) are wearable passive samplers that provide time-integrated measurements of personal exposure to a range of airborne environmental contaminants (SI.3)https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?bMTyAZ Participants were also provided with PurpleAir Touch monitors to measure indoor PM 2.5 mass concentration(SI.4)https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?6rxail

table.header: PERSONAL BIOSPECIMEN COLLECTION AND EXPOSURE MONITORS

table.text: Participants were recruited through social media advertisements and completed an eligibility survey REDCap).
All participants provided informed consent.
Participants were shipped study kits via UPS Next Day Air containing (1) an indoor PurpleAir monitor, (2) a setup guide, and (3) a pre-labeled UPS LabPak for sample return.
Upon receiving the kit, participants were instructed to install the PurpleAir monitor in their home (any room except kitchen) and operate it continuously for the duration of the study.
Participants were instructed to abstain from ejaculation for 2-5 days prior to the in-person visit.

Participants completed a post-sampling survey assessing ease of use, comfort with each collection platform and setting, recent exposure to poor outdoor air quality, smoking habits, and recreational activities.
The remaining 18 participants completed PurpleAir monitor setup, surveys, in-person pre-event baseline, and at-home pre-event semen and blood baseline collection 5-7 days later.
table.header: High participant retention across multiple sampling timepoints

table.text: Sixteen participants completed sampling and surveys during the post-event resample.
table.header: High participant retention across multiple sampling timepoints

table.text: Of the nine participants assigned to wear FAWs, six returned their post-event wristband.
table.header: High participant retention across multiple sampling timepoints

table.text: All 18 participants completed the pre-scheduled baselines (At-Clinic and At-Home Pre-Event), while 16/18 completed the Post-Event Resampling despite receiving only one day's notice of package delivery and a few days' notice of sampling.
In survey responses regarding semen collection, participants were less likely to indicate that the test was awkward or embarrassing to perform when collecting at home.

However, for the PurpleAir monitors, participants were not uniformly in agreement that the monitor data was easy to understand, presenting an opportunity for future studies to include a data literacy component.
Participants had the flexibility to sample and answer surveys when convenient without travel burdens.

We want to thank our participants for volunteering their time and effort for this study, Connie Pete for initial sample processing and Kathy Winter for their assistance at the Center for Research in Reproduction and Contraception (CRRC) at the University of Washington.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

live_data_statements: • Results: 18 participants completed the initial in-person and scheduled at-home sampling, and 16 (89%) completed subsequent remote sampling.
Participants were willing to provide a median of 18 semen samples (range, 2-40) and 18 blood samples (range, 5-40) over a future hypothetical study.

To do this, we enrolled reproductive age men in a dual clinical/remote study in which participants self-collected blood using the homeRNA platform and semen using the Fellow kit, continuously monitored home indoor PM 2.5 mass concentration estimates using PurpleAir monitors, and, in a subset of participants, passively sampled environmental organic chemical exposures continuously over a seven day period using Fresh Air wristbands.

By combining these remote collection protocols, we evaluated the feasibility of a multi-biofluid collection study with multiple timepoints where, during wildfire season, enrolled participants provided one baseline sample in-clinic and up to three samples remotely.

The Fellow Semen Analysis Kit (Fellow) is a semen analysis platform that enables at-home semen collection, stabilization, and shipment for laboratory semen analysis (SI.1)https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?RMhwhy 24,25) The homeRNAmax Blood Collection and Stabilization Kit (homeRNA) combines a commercially available peripheral blood collection device with a custom-engineered stabilization tube (SI.2)https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?Hqmpgm Fresh Air wristbands (FAW) are wearable passive samplers that provide time-integrated measurements of personal exposure to a range of airborne environmental contaminants (SI.3)https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?bMTyAZ Participants were also provided with PurpleAir Touch monitors to measure indoor PM 2.5 mass concentration(SI.4)https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?6rxail
Participants were recruited through social media advertisements and completed an eligibility survey REDCap).
All participants provided informed consent.
Participants were shipped study kits via UPS Next Day Air containing (1) an indoor PurpleAir monitor, (2) a setup guide, and (3) a pre-labeled UPS LabPak for sample return.
Upon receiving the kit, participants were instructed to install the PurpleAir monitor in their home (any room except kitchen) and operate it continuously for the duration of the study.
Participants were instructed to abstain from ejaculation for 2-5 days prior to the in-person visit.

Participants completed a post-sampling survey assessing ease of use, comfort with each collection platform and setting, recent exposure to poor outdoor air quality, smoking habits, and recreational activities.
The remaining 18 participants completed PurpleAir monitor setup, surveys, in-person pre-event baseline, and at-home pre-event semen and blood baseline collection 5-7 days later.
Sixteen participants completed sampling and surveys during the post-event resample.
Of the nine participants assigned to wear FAWs, six returned their post-event wristband.

All 18 participants completed the pre-scheduled baselines (At-Clinic and At-Home Pre-Event), while 16/18 completed the Post-Event Resampling despite receiving only one day's notice of package delivery and a few days' notice of sampling.
In survey responses regarding semen collection, participants were less likely to indicate that the test was awkward or embarrassing to perform when collecting at home.

However, for the PurpleAir monitors, participants were not uniformly in agreement that the monitor data was easy to understand, presenting an opportunity for future studies to include a data literacy component.
Participants had the flexibility to sample and answer surveys when convenient without travel burdens.

We want to thank our participants for volunteering their time and effort for this study, Connie Pete for initial sample processing and Kathy Winter for their assistance at the Center for Research in Reproduction and Contraception (CRRC) at the University of Washington.
